A standard upright piano holds roughly eighteen tons of tension. Emil liked to remind himself of that whenever he rested his forearm against a polished cheek block. Beneath the mahogany veneer and the polite domesticity of ivory and felt, steel wires were pulling against a cast-iron harp with the force of a small bridge. It was a machine built to hold an argument in suspension, and every six months or so, the weather won a little ground.

By the time he reached Mara’s third-floor walk-up, the November rain had soaked through the shoulders of his wool coat. The apartment smelled of cardboard and lemon oil. Nearly everything was packed. Towers of taped boxes lined the baseboards, and pale rectangles marked the walls where framed photographs had spent the last twenty years. Only the piano remained—a dark walnut upright from 1928, sitting square against the plaster like an anchor too heavy to haul aboard.

"The community center is sending a truck Thursday," Mara said, taking his umbrella and setting it in a cracked ceramic crock by the door. She looked to be in her late sixties, wearing a cardigan with the sleeves pushed up to her elbows. "I know it’ll go out again once they bounce it down the stairs. I just didn’t want to hand them a sour thing."

Emil nodded. He liked clients like this. Most people waited until a string snapped or a key stuck down like a bad tooth. Paying to tune an instrument you were giving away was a quiet, almost obsolete kind of grace.

He knelt beside the bench and unrolled his canvas tool kit: the rosewood-handled tuning lever, a wedge of gray rubber mutes, a long ribbon of red felt. When he lifted the top lid and unlatched the front panel, the interior exhaled a familiar, dusty warmth—aged spruce, old glue, sheep’s wool, oxidized brass. He pulled the bottom kickboard as well, kneeling to check the pedal linkages, and found the usual domestic archaeology tucked beside the bass bridge: a petrified rubber band, two tarnished pennies, a cedar pencil chewed down to the ferrule, and a single blue glass marble clouded with white swirls.

He set the marble on the music desk. Mara picked it up and rolled it between her fingers. "My nephew’s," she said softly. "He’s thirty now. Lives in Seattle."

Emil struck his A440 tuning fork against his knee and pressed the stem to the wooden rim until the pitch bloomed faintly in the bare room. He threaded the red felt strip between the outer wires of the middle octave, muting them so he could isolate each center string. Then he fit the socket of his lever onto the first steel pin and began to listen.

Tuning was less about hearing notes than hearing the friction between them. When two strings disagreed, the air pulsed with a seasick wobble—*beats*, tuners called them. *Wah-wah-wah.* As Emil leaned his weight carefully into the lever, nudging the pin a fraction of a millimeter, the wobble slowed, stretched out, and finally flattened into clean glass. He worked methodically across the middle register, setting the foundation, his left hand tapping the keys in steady, hypnotic pairs while his right hand negotiated with iron and wire.

Halfway through, Mara brought him a mug of black tea. The mugs were mismatched; the good set, she apologized, was already wrapped in newspaper. She leaned against a stack of boxes and watched him work.

"My brother used to ask why tuners don't just use a little screen," she said. "Like the ones guitarists clip on."

"Some do," Emil said, pausing to take a sip. The tea was scalding and bright. "They’re fine for a rough pass if the room is loud. But a meter only knows arithmetic. A piano isn't quite arithmetic."

"No?"

"If you tune every fifth mathematically pure," Emil said, touching two keys so a clear, hollow interval rang out, "and you climb all the way around the twelve notes back to where you started, you overshoot. The circle doesn't close. There's a little sliver left over—a gap called the Pythagorean comma. Nature refuses to make the math come out even."

Mara tilted her head. "So what do you do?"

"You cheat," Emil said gently. "You shave a tiny fraction off every fifth, just enough that the ear forgives it. You spread the imperfection evenly across the whole keyboard. Nothing is completely pure, so that everything can bear to live in the same room."

She looked around the stripped apartment—at the bare floorboards, the stacked boxes, the rain bead-tracking down the uncurtained glass. "That sounds about right," she murmured.

The last hour passed in a climb of octaves. In the high treble, the short steel wires rang like cold drops of water striking tin; down in the bass, the thick copper-wound strings groaned awake and settled into a deep, resonant growl. Without rugs or bookshelves to swallow the sound, the whole apartment acted like an extension of the soundboard.

When he finished, Emil pulled the last rubber mute, fitted the panels back into place, and wiped the keys with a square of flannel. He didn't play concert pieces—tuners rarely did—so he simply laid his hands on the keyboard and pressed a slow C-major ninth, holding the damper pedal down. The chord rose and filled the empty corners, warm and luminous, balanced entirely on its deliberate, microscopic lies.

At the door, while he buttoned his coat, Mara pressed the blue marble into his palm. "For your collection," she said.

He didn't have one, though he didn't tell her that. Outside, the rain had thinned to a cold mist. Emil walked toward the bus stop with his canvas roll tucked under his arm, turning the smooth glass against his thumb, listening to the damp city hum around him in a thousand competing keys.
